sources.title: Edward Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
sources.locator: arXiv:2106.09685v2; §4.1–4.2 and the opening of §5, PDF pp. 3–5. The full 26-page PDF was opened; §4.1's frozen-base and rank-factorized update, its zero-B initialization, exact merge, and the scope at the start of §5 were inspected. No specific benchmark result is imported.

contents.name: The frozen base matrix and trainable low-rank factors define an update W0+BA, with the same input passed through base and update branches.
LoRA initializes B at zero and merges the factor product into the base weight for inference; the local algorithm fixes its own finite gradient-descent schedule.
The real-arithmetic identity W0x+BAx=(W0+BA)x is the source convention for exact merging; the local proof handles general nonzero real scale c.

The paper presents low intrinsic rank as motivation and reports experiments under specific model/data settings; no universal low-rank task-transfer, convergence, latency, or memory theorem is imported.

sources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 18.S096, Matrix Calculus for Machine Learning and Beyond, Lecture 5 Part 3: Forward and Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation
sources.locator: Complete 16-page lecture note fetched; relevant complete reasoning read in §8.3, PDF pp. 8–11, on computational-graph reverse accumulation and summing contributions from all downstream uses, and §8.4, PDF pp. 11–12, on scalar objectives, reverse-mode cost orientation, and tape conventions.

contents.name: A finite differentiable scalar computation graph is evaluated forward and differentiated backward, with all downstream-use contributions summed at a shared input.

Reverse accumulation computes the derivative of a scalar objective with respect to many inputs; the local matrix-gradient formulas are independently derived by the chain rule and Frobenius trace identities.

sources.title: Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition
sources.locator: §7E, Theorems 7.70 and 7.80, printed pp. 273–277 (PDF pp. 286–290). The SVD theorem and proof, and the matrix factorization theorem and proof, were read in full. The finite real SVD supplies the positive singular-value decomposition used to construct balanced factors, with zero rows and columns padding ranks below r.

contents.name: The finite-dimensional SVD represents a real linear map by positive singular values and orthonormal domain/range vectors; the proof identifies the number of positive singular values with the image rank.
The matrix SVD gives an explicit factorization from the positive singular-value terms; splitting each value into two square roots yields factors of the required shapes.
